title: Aftermarket driver assist under federal probe following fatal crashes
gist: NHTSA's Office of Defects Investigation opened a preliminary evaluation into comma.ai's aftermarket driver-assist devices after five crashes (three deaths, 11 injuries) in which comma.ai-controlled vehicles, including ones running unofficial forks like FrogPilot, failed to detect stopped or merging vehicles; comma's openpilot software now supports 325+ models across 27 brands with over 30,000 users and 402 million miles driven.

insights.claim: NHTSA's Office of Defects Investigation opened a probe after identifying five crashes involving comma.ai driver-assist devices, resulting in three deaths across two crashes and 11 injuries across four of the five crashes.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: A federal preliminary evaluation is the first regulatory step that can lead to a recall or mandatory restrictions on aftermarket ADAS devices, a direct regulatory risk for comma.ai and any similar aftermarket driver-assist vendors.
insights.locator: The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s Office of Defects Investigation

insights.claim: NHTSA says it isn't sure comma.ai's systems can adequately detect a slow or stopped car in the path of travel; at least two of the five crashes involved a comma.ai-controlled car hitting a stopped vehicle, including one crash into a first responder's vehicle that killed three people.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Stopped-object detection failure is a known hard problem for camera/radar-only ADAS stacks (echoes past Tesla Autopilot stopped-vehicle crash investigations), suggesting a systemic technical limitation rather than a one-off bug.
insights.locator: But NHTSA isn’t sure that Comma’s systems

insights.claim: NHTSA is specifically interested in which software version was running during each crash, noting at least two of the five crashes involved unofficial forks of the main openpilot build, including the fatal crash, which was running a fork called FrogPilot.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Open-source forking of safety-critical driver-assist software (unofficial builds like FrogPilot running in a fatal crash) raises a liability and oversight question unique to open-source ADAS business models versus closed OEM systems.
insights.locator: NHTSA says it is also interested in which version

insights.claim: Comma.ai was founded by George Hotz, known for jailbreaking iOS and hacking Sony PlayStations, who in 2015 began modifying his own Acura with an advanced driver assist system, originally intending to sell the system to Tesla as a Mobileye replacement.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Provides founder/origin context relevant to assessing comma.ai's engineering culture and risk tolerance (hacker background, direct Tesla/Mobileye rivalry ambitions).
insights.locator: Comma.ai was the brainchild of George Hotz

insights.claim: After NHTSA began asking questions in 2016 about Comma's plans to sell plug-in OBD-port devices, Comma pivoted to open-sourcing its openpilot software and hardware plans on GitHub, letting anyone build the devices themselves; by 2020 its software and $999 device were rated more highly by Consumer Reports than any OEM system.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Comma's open-source, DIY-hardware model was originally a regulatory workaround, which may now complicate NHTSA's ability to impose conventional recall/liability remedies since anyone can build and modify the hardware/software independently.
insights.locator: Comma’s first attempts to sell devices

insights.claim: Comma's current device, the Comma Four, supports lane centering, adaptive cruise, and a cloud-based dash cam across more than 325 car models from 27 different brands, with more than 30,000 drivers using openpilot and over 402 million miles (650 million km) driven.
insights.speaker: Jonathan M. Gitlin
insights.so_what: Scale metrics (30,000+ users, 402M+ miles) show a real installed base and safety-relevant exposure, giving investors/regulators a denominator against which to assess the five-crash incident rate.
insights.locator: Now, Comma says the Comma Four can add lane centering
